title: WATCHERS OF WHAT IS HAPPENING

publication_scope.included: External public evidence, GitHub staff statements, public repository controls, witness comparisons, falsifiers, and calibrated hypotheses.
publication_scope.excluded: Internal JANUS implementation, maintenance, debugging, cleanup, and local engineering diagnostics not required to reproduce external evidence.

breakthrough.finding: GitHub staff publicly confirmed a January 2026 server-side schedule registration/synchronization failure with the same broad symptom family.
breakthrough.importance: This turns 'stale or lost schedule registration' from a purely community-level hypothesis into a previously demonstrated GitHub-side failure mechanism, while not proving that the August case has the identical root cause.

staff_statements.finding: A recently enabled server-side feature flag caused the issue for newly created scheduled workflows. The flag was disabled; pushing a new change to the repository was expected to repair affected schedule workflows.
GitHub identified a related change from the previous week and rolled it back. A commit pushed to the default branch would resync impacted scheduled workflows.

When a scheduled job is dropped early enough, there is currently no visible evidence because processing has not advanced far enough to create the underlying artifacts shown to users; GitHub described this as a UX gap and said work was underway to improve it.

mechanistic_model_supported_by_precedent: schedule definition exists and workflow is visible/active
schedule registration or synchronization becomes stale/broken server-side
workflow_dispatch and push can remain healthy because they use different trigger paths
no run object/artifact may appear for a scheduled fire that is dropped before deeper processing
default-branch activity can cause schedule metadata to be resynchronized after the underlying server-side problem is removed

observations: New repositories on an established Free personal account were tested as both private and public.
Manual execution worked while scheduled execution never fired initially.
The thread accumulated independent reports from multiple users with the same trigger-path split.
common_with_august_cohort: recovery can occur after server-side rollback and re-registration

observations: Actions had worked for almost a year.
For roughly three days new workflows stopped triggering, while workflows that had successfully triggered before the issue continued to run.
january_2026_witness_cohort.relevance: Points specifically toward creation/registration state rather than generic runner unavailability.

observations: schedule failed for more than 24 hours while workflow_dispatch and push worked.
After GitHub-side rollback, editing YAML to re-register and running again restored scheduling.
A minimal */5 scheduled workflow never triggered.
No job logs or runner diagnostic evidence existed because the scheduled trigger itself never occurred.
january_2026_witness_cohort.common_with_august_cohort: Failure occurs before runner participation, showing GitHub-hosted runner capacity is not required for this failure class.

reported_fingerprint: multiple non-top-of-hour cron expressions were tested
timeline: At approximately 15:19 UTC on 2026-07-30 the public Actions API still showed total_count=0 for event=schedule.
The first scheduled run was later observed around 17:05 UTC without a repository-side explanation for the earlier absence.
Current API history for 2026-07-30 through 2026-07-31 contains 27 scheduled runs, confirming recovery rather than a permanently invalid workflow.
common_with_janus_reference: scheduled and non-scheduled trigger paths coexist
GitHub Pages is part of the workflow surface
the decisive symptom is absence/delay before user job execution

observations: One workflow fired successfully once at 2026-07-28 22:45:16 UTC and then missed eight or more expected cron matches.
A second workflow had never scheduled despite five or more expected matches.
workflow_dispatch worked repeatedly for both workflows.
Touching both workflow files did not immediately restore expected scheduling.
Scheduling later partially recovered on its own but only intermittently, roughly one fire every several hours rather than the configured hourly cadence.
additional_july_2026_control.relevance: A degradation path of healthy -> missing schedules -> partial spontaneous recovery predates the August incident and resembles the later delay/escalation pattern more closely than a never-registered new repository alone.

interpretive_update.previous_model: August 26 may have left residual damage in scheduled-workflow materialization.
interpretive_update.new_model: GitHub has at least two documented schedule failure mechanisms that can look identical from outside: high-load dropping before user-visible artifacts, and server-side registration/synchronization bugs affecting schedules while other trigger paths remain healthy. The August cohort may involve either, a combination, or another related implementation defect.
why_august_is_still_special: JANUS and drakedog-kr show escalation from tens-of-minutes delays to multi-hour delays rather than only first-registration failure.
shinkunda shows a previously functioning repository losing all schedule run creation after August 26.
GitHub officially reported trigger-database saturation and a later incident in which some workflow runs failed to trigger.
The August timing supports amplification by platform stress, but does not identify the exact schedule-registration code path.

updated_hypotheses.hypothesis: No-run-object scheduled failures are impossible unless user YAML is wrong.
A GitHub-side stale/lost schedule registration state is technically possible.
A dropped schedule can leave no user-visible run evidence.
The August 26 event used exactly the same January feature-flag bug.
August 26 stress amplified an existing scheduler-registration/materialization weakness.

next_collection_gates: Search GitHub staff replies and changelogs between January and August for later scheduler-registration changes or rollbacks.
Build a dated cohort separating NEW_WORKFLOW_REGISTRATION, PREVIOUSLY_HEALTHY_THEN_STOPPED, MULTIHOUR_DELAY, and EARLY_DROP_NO_ARTIFACT.
Check whether August witnesses recover after a default-branch commit or schedule rewrite; treat recovery as a discriminator, not an automatic fix recommendation.
Continue to keep cross-provider and Russian-service observations separate unless a technical common dependency or IOC appears.
